boilerplate.section_intro: This section consists of questions and problems involving quantitative reasoning.  Each question is followed by four possible responses.  Choose the correct answer and mark its number in the appropriate place on the answer sheet.
boilerplate.section_meta:
This section contains 20 questions.
The time allotted is 20 minutes.
boilerplate.gray_note: Note:  The words appearing against a gray background are translated into several languages at the bottom of each page.
boilerplate.general_comments_title: General Comments about the Quantitative Reasoning Section
general_comments: The figures accompanying some of the problems are provided to help solve the problems, but are not necessarily drawn to scale.  Therefore, do not rely on the figures alone to deduce line length, angle size, and so forth.
If a line in a figure appears to be straight, you may assume that it is in fact a straight line.
When a geometric term (side, radius, area, volume, etc.) appears in a problem, it refers to a term whose value is greater than 0, unless stated otherwise.
When \(\sqrt{a}\) (a > 0) appears in a problem, it refers to the positive root of a.
"0" is neither a positive nor a negative number.

clusters.intro: Study the graph below, then answer the four questions that follow. The graph below describes a circular hiking trail in the mountains. The letters A through I indicate points along the trail. Each point on the trail is marked with a circle next to which its elevation (above sea level) in meters appears. Some of the points are overnight points (see key). The length of the section of the trail connecting each two points is indicated in the graph (in km). The table below the graph presents the estimated walking times (in hours) between each two adjacent points. The upper row presents the estimated walking times when walking clockwise, and the lower row – when walking counterclockwise. For example: Point B, which is at an elevation of 1,500 meters, is an overnight point. The length of the section of the trail connecting it to point A is 7 km. The estimated walking time from point B to point A, counterclockwise, is 2.5 hours.

Study the table below, then answer the five questions that follow.

The table presents data on the 8 printing jobs that were done at a print shop on a certain day between 5:00 and 15:40.  The jobs are marked with the letters A-H.  In each printing job an item of a certain type was printed in some number of copies.
For each printing job the table presents: the type of item that was printed (book, journal, poster or booklet), the total number of pages that was printed, the start time of the job, the end time of the job and the number of breaks during the printing (the printing presses do not necessarily print continuously and there may be breaks in their operation).  In addition, the last column of the table records the degree of urgency of the job (low, medium, high or very high).
During the period of time that elapsed from the start time of the job until the end time of the job (including the breaks), the job is in “printing processes”.

questions.stem:
a and b are consecutive numbers  (a < b).

Given:  4a = 3b

b = ?

methods.text: Consecutive with \(a<b\) means \(b = a+1\), so \(4a = 3a+3\) and \(a = 3\), giving \(b = 4\).
Test each option as \(b\): \(b=4\) needs \(a=3\), and \(4 \times 3 = 3 \times 4\) ✓. The others fail immediately.

questions.stem: Which of the following polygons is a polygon whose perimeter can be calculated, if only its area is given?

Efrat wants to enter her room. She is outside the building, and therefore she needs to open the door of the building, the door of her apartment and the door of the room. All the doors are locked, and each door has a different key. Efrat tries to open the doors with the help of the three keys, but she does not remember which of them opens which door. Efrat does not try to open any door with a key that she already knows does not fit it. How many attempts to open a door with a key will Efrat make, at most, until she enters her room (an attempt that succeeds – in which the door opens – is also counted as an attempt)?

Dvir and Harel are eating ice cream, each at his own fixed rate.  Dvir's rate of eating is 2 times as much as Harel's rate of eating.
Together they finish eating \(\frac{1}{4}\) of a box of ice cream in 10 minutes.

In how many minutes would Harel finish eating a whole box of ice cream, if he were eating on his own?

methods.text: Together they do \(\frac14\) of a box in 10 minutes, so \(\frac{1}{40}\) a minute. Dvir is twice Harel, so Harel is a third of that: \(\frac{1}{120}\).
A full box therefore takes Harel 120 minutes. Splitting a combined rate in the given ratio — not in half — is the step the options are built around.

questions.stem:
How many two-digit positive numbers satisfy the following two conditions?
a. The sum of the digits of the number equals 5
b. The number is prime

methods.text: Digit sum 5 gives only 14, 23, 32, 41 and 50. Five candidates, and now test each for primality.
14 and 32 are even, 50 ends in 0, so all three are composite immediately. That leaves 23 ✓ and 41 ✓ — both prime. Two numbers.

questions.stem:
The letters A, B, C and D represent digits between 1 and 9 (not necessarily different from one another), such that AB, BA and CD are two-digit numbers.

Given:  AB + BA = CD

C – D = ?
options: It cannot be determined from the information given

methods.text: \(\overline{AB} + \overline{BA} = (10A+B) + (10B+A) = 11(A+B)\). So \(\overline{CD}\) is a multiple of 11, and a two-digit multiple of 11 always has equal digits.

\(C = D\), so \(C - D = 0\) — and it never mattered what \(A\) and \(B\) actually were. Reversing a two-digit number and adding always gives a multiple of 11; subtracting always gives a multiple of 9.

questions.stem:
Roi registered for 6 courses, in each of which there are 5 meetings.
Roi failed every course in which he participated in 2 meetings or fewer,
and passed every course in which he participated in 3 meetings or more.
It is known that Roi failed 3 courses and passed 3 courses.

Roi participated in at least ______ meetings and at most ______ meetings.

methods.text: The three failed courses contribute between 0 and 2 meetings each; the three passed contribute between 3 and 5. So the minimum is \(0+9 = 9\) and the maximum is \(6+15 = 21\).
Every wrong option gets one end right and one wrong, so both ends have to be computed — the minimum is not \(3 \times 3 + 3 \times 3\), because a failed course can have zero meetings.

questions.stem:
Keren, Shlomit and Tamara divided a pile of coins among themselves.

Given:  \(\dfrac{\text{the number of coins that Keren received}}{\text{the number of coins that Tamara received}} = \dfrac{5}{9}\)

\(\dfrac{\text{the number of coins that Shlomit received}}{\text{the number of coins that Tamara received}} = \dfrac{5}{12}\)

\(\dfrac{\text{the number of coins that Keren and Shlomit received together}}{\text{the number of coins that Tamara received}} = ?\)

methods.text: Chain the ratios so the shared name cancels, exactly as with \(p:q:r\) chains. The product of the two given ratios is \(\frac{35}{36}\).
Build one consistent set of counts from the two ratios and read the answer off directly — slower, but it works when the chaining direction is hard to see.

questions.stem:
Given:  0 < a  ,  \(\frac{21-3a}{2a+1} < 0\)

Which of the following inequalities is necessarily true?

methods.text: \(a\) is positive, so \(2a+1\) is positive and the sign of the quotient is the sign of the numerator alone. \(21-3a<0\) gives \(a>7\).
One known sign collapses the whole sign analysis into a single inequality. Without the given \(0<a\) this would need a two-case split; with it there is only one case.
The only place the quotient can change sign, given \(a>0\), is where the numerator vanishes — at \(a=7\). Only one option starts exactly there.

questions.stem:
For every positive integer k,
the expression  \((k!) \cdot 2^k\)  is equal to the product of all the –

methods.text: Write \(k!\cdot2^k\) as \((1\cdot2\cdot3\cdots k)\) with one factor of 2 handed to each term: \((1\cdot2)(2\cdot2)(3\cdot2)\cdots(k\cdot2)\), which is \(2\cdot4\cdot6\cdots2k\) — every even number up to \(2k\).
Take \(k=3\): \(3!\cdot2^3=6\cdot8=48\). Now check the options. Integers 1 to 6 give 720 ✗. Even numbers 2 to 6 give \(2\cdot4\cdot6=48\) ✓. One small value settles it.

questions.stem:
The average height of Orit, Batya and Gili is 4 cm lower than the average height of all the children in their class.  Orit's height is 6 cm lower than the average height in the class.

The average height of Batya and Gili is ______ the average height in the class.

In the accompanying figure there is a circle whose center is O and whose radius is r, and a rectangle ABCD.
Side BC is tangent to the circle at point E.
Straight line OD intersects side BC at point F.

Given:  EC = CD = 2r

Based on this information,
EF = ?

methods.text: Over the common denominator \((3+\sqrt3)(3-\sqrt3) = 6\), the numerator is \((3-\sqrt3)^2+(3+\sqrt3)^2 = 24\), since the cross terms cancel. So the value is 4.
A fraction plus its own reciprocal: the surds are arranged to disappear, which is why the answer is a plain integer.

questions.stem:
a is any negative number.

a + | a | = ?

methods.text: For a negative number, \(|a|=-a\). So \(a+|a|\) is \(a-a\), which is 0.
\(a=-5\): \(-5+5=0\). Any negative value gives the same thing.

questions.stem:
In a soccer game the two teams scored 20 goals altogether.
Given:  – Aviad himself scored half of the number of goals that his team scored.
– The number of goals that Aviad scored is smaller by 2 than the number of goals that the opposing team scored.

How many goals did Aviad's team score in the game?

methods.text: Let \(T\) be Aviad's team's goals. Aviad scored \(\frac T2\), and the opposing team scored \(20 - T\). The second condition gives \(\frac T2 = (20-T) - 2\), so \(\frac{3T}{2} = 18\) and \(T = 12\).
\(T=12\): Aviad scored 6, the opposition scored 8, and \(6 = 8-2\) ✓. Each option takes one line to check.

questions.stem: Nivi has a box with 200 cubes in it. 70% of the cubes are purple, and 30% are yellow. Nivi received another 40 purple cubes and added them to the box. What is the percentage of the yellow cubes in the box now?

methods.text: The yellow count never changes: \(30\%\) of 200 is 60. Only the total moves, from 200 to 240. So yellow is \(\frac{60}{240} = 25\%\).
Adding purple cubes cannot change how many yellow there are — it changes the base. Watching which of the two numbers moves is the whole question.

15 empty jars that are numbered from 1 to 15 are arranged in a row according to the order of their numbers.
Romi placed one coin in each jar, then she placed a coin in each jar whose number is divisible by 2, then – in each jar whose number is divisible by 3, and so on up to 15.

The number of coins in jar 14 ______ in jar 2.
options: is the same as their number
is twice as much as their number
is three times as much as their number
is four times as much as their number

methods.text: Jar \(n\) receives one coin for every number that divides \(n\) — so the coins in jar \(n\) equal its number of divisors.
Summing divisor counts from 1 to 15 gives 1, 2, 2, 3, 2, 4, 2, 4, 3, 4, 2, 6, 2, 4, 4 — a total of 45, which is three times the 15 jars.

questions.stem:
Alona and Shira are playing a game.  In each round each of them tosses a dice.
If the numbers that were obtained are different from one another, they play another round.  Otherwise, the game ends.

What is the probability that the game will end after exactly two rounds?

Given:  4x – 2xy + 3y = 74

\(\frac{x}{2} + \frac{xy}{3} - \frac{y}{2} = -\frac{2}{3}\)

x = ?

methods.text: Multiply the second equation by 6: \(3x + 2xy - 3y = -4\). Adding it to the first, the \(xy\) and \(y\) terms cancel and \(7x = 70\), so \(x = 10\).

Two equations containing an \(xy\) term look nonlinear and frightening. Clearing the fractions first makes the cross terms opposites, and addition removes them — scaling to make terms cancel is the move.

questions.stem:
x and y are positive integers that are divisible by 3.

What is the largest number that the sum (x+y) is certainly divisible by?

methods.text: \(x = 3a\) and \(y = 3b\), so \(x + y = 3(a+b)\) — always a multiple of 3, and that is all that is forced.
Two cases kill the rest. \(x=y=3\) gives 6, which is not divisible by 9 or 12; \(x=3,\ y=6\) gives 9, which is not divisible by 6. Only 3 survives both.

questions.stem: How many circles different from one another whose circumference (in cm) is a positive integer and whose area (in cm²) is also a positive integer exist?

Itzhak travels at a fixed speed of 70 kph.
Rut travels at a fixed speed of 105 kph.
Rut travels y km in a third of the time in which Itzhak travels x km.

Which of the following statements is true?

methods.text: Itzhak's time for \(x\) km is \(\frac x{70}\). Rut travels for \(\frac{x}{210}\) hours at 105, covering \(y = \frac{105x}{210} = \frac x2\), so \(2y = x\).
Take \(x = 210\): Itzhak needs 3 hours, so Rut travels for 1 hour and covers 105. \(2(105) = 210\) ✓. Choosing \(x\) as a multiple of both 70 and 3 makes every number whole.
